title: Record the wrongs, then stand still to see God’s salvation
setting: Joseph Smith wrote this in the jail at Liberty, Missouri, in an undated letter of about 22 March 1839. His fellow prisoners also signed it. The letter went to Bishop Edward Partridge and the Church, by way of Quincy, Illinois, where many Saints had fled. The Saints had lost homes, land, and lives in the Missouri conflict of 1838. The letter recalls the killings at Hawn’s Mill and the death of apostle David Patten.
summary: The letter suggests the Saints gather the facts of their suffering in Missouri. They should record property losses and injuries to character and person. They should list the names of those who oppressed them. A committee might take statements and affidavits and collect libelous publications. The goal is to publish the record and present it to the heads of government. The letter calls this an “imperative duty” to God, to families, to widows and orphans, and to the rising generation. Many people of all faiths, it says, miss the truth only because they do not know where to find it. It ends by urging the Saints to do all they can, then stand still and trust God.

contextNote.title: Truth hidden for want of a guide
contextNote.text: The Saints had been driven out, and verses 4–5 note that many published accounts were hostile. Verse 12 explains why gathering the facts matters beyond the Saints themselves. Many people in every church are “only kept from the truth” because they “know not where to find it”. Verse 13 draws the result: the Saints should wear out their lives bringing hidden things to light. Verse 16 adds that a very small helm can steer a large ship in a storm. In this passage, careful record-keeping is a way to make the truth findable for others.

ldsText: The 2025 Come, Follow Me lesson for sections 121–123 draws attention to the small helm in verse 16. What does verse 17 ask the Saints to do before they “stand still,” and what does it promise afterward?

jsp.title: Letter to Edward Partridge and the Church, circa 22 March 1839

reviewNote: Read all 17 verses. Official heading: Liberty jail, about 22 March 1839, an excerpt from the epistle to the Church on the Saints' duties toward their persecutors. JSP historical introduction read; it confirms the letter recalls the Hawn's Mill and David W. Patten deaths and tells the Saints to prepare affidavits of their Missouri losses. Patten is not named in the section text itself. Fact-check 2026-10-12: setting notes the letter is undated and signed by the fellow prisoners, softens “most” Saints at Quincy, and drops an unsupported claim that petitions had failed.
